# The problem
<!--
Outlining the issue / weak point / problem to be solved by this
proposal. This should be a compelling section that sets the reader up

It is important to cover:

 - [ ] What the problem is
 - [ ] Who it affects
 - [ ] Why is it a problem

Performance regressions can slip past unit tests and harm software, increasing runtime or memory usage. R package developers need a way to estimate how much a change affected performance. However, on most development machines and on CI runners, runtime measurements are noisy enough that distinguishing between normal variation and a real effect can be very challenging. One way to reduce that noise is to measure baseline and candidate revisions on the same machine, which reduces machine-to-machine variation [@laaberCloud2019].

R packages often rely on compiled code or multiprocessing in order to speed up computation, which proves to be a problem for memory measurement; tracking R-level allocations will not capture true memory usage in these kinds of workloads. Reliable revision-level runtime and memory comparisons would let developers detect and investigate these regressions before they reach users, without requiring dedicated benchmarking hardware.

Existing R tools address parts of this problem: `bench` measures runtime and R allocation behavior [@bench], `cross` runs expressions across package versions or Git branches [@cross], and `atime` measures runtime and R-level memory across both package versions and data sizes, making it useful for detecting differences in asymptotic scaling [@atime; @atimePaper]. `atime` can also compare multiple relevant package versions. `touchstone` comes closest to a paired revision experiment [@touchstone], and is already used in a variety of R packages. None of these tools combine process-tree peak memory and support arbitrary benchmark commands (see @sec-existing-tools).
